summary.text: Cosmic inflation is a theory that space expanded exponentially fast in the very early universe.
The expansion supercooled the universe and ended when the energy of the field driving it condensed into hot, dense particles, a process called reheating.
Quantum fluctuations in a microscopic region were magnified to cosmic size and became the seeds for the growth of structure in the universe.

facts.label: Growth in size
facts.value: Radius grew from about 4 × 10⁻²⁹ m to about 0.9 m

facts.label: Hypothetical field
facts.value: The field thought to drive it is the inflaton

facts.label: Kavli Prize
facts.value: Starobinsky, Guth and Linde won it in 2014

items.prompt: Picture a hot, expanding cloud of matter spread perfectly smoothly. Why would stars struggle to form in it?

options.label: Hot clouds always turn into pure light before stars form
A uniform spread has no force to pull matter into clumps
Even clouds collapse too quickly to make separate stars
Expansion only acts on clouds that are unevenly dense

items.explain: Clumping needs density contrast, and a completely uniform density has no force to drive it.

items.prompt: Inflation stretched microscopic ripples to enormous size. What role did those ripples play afterward?

options.label: They were the particles that made up the first stars
They stopped the expansion once they grew big enough
They carried the energy that drove the expansion
They became the seeds for the growth of structure

items.explain: Quantum fluctuations magnified to cosmic size became the seeds for the growth of structure in the universe.

items.prompt: When inflation ended, what happened to the field that had been driving it?

options.label: Its energy condensed into hot, dense particles
It switched on a faster second round of expansion
It spread out evenly until nothing was left of it
It was captured by stars forming in the universe

items.explain: Inflation ended when the energy of the driving field condensed into hot, dense particles, called reheating.

items.prompt: Observations show the universe is flat to within a few percent, and expansion makes the universe flatter over time. What does that imply about the early universe?

options.label: It must have been strongly curved at first
Its flatness then was a matter of chance
It must have been exceptionally close to flat
It could not be compared with the present universe

items.explain: Because expansion increases flatness, the early universe must have been exceptionally close to flat.

items.prompt: Particle theories predict heavy magnetic charges should dominate the universe, yet none are found. How could inflation account for that?

options.label: Inflation would destroy each one when it ended
Expansion would spread them apart, lowering their density
Inflation would turn them into ordinary particles
Expansion would pack them together out of view

items.explain: A period of inflation below the temperature where monopoles form would separate them as the universe expands, lowering their observed density.

items.prompt: A physicist claims we know exactly which particle-physics process drove inflation, and that every scientist accepts the theory. What is wrong?

options.label: The detailed mechanism is unknown, and some scientists dissent
No observation has ever matched anything the theory predicts
The theory says inflation lasted exactly 10⁻³⁵ seconds
The theory was only proposed after the year 2000

items.explain: The detailed particle physics mechanism is unknown, and some scientists dissent from the view that observations support inflation.

paragraphs.heading: What inflation is
paragraphs.text: Cosmic inflation is the idea that in the very early universe, space expanded exponentially fast. During it, the distance between points doubled every 10⁻³⁷ seconds, and the phase lasted at least 10⁻³⁵ seconds, though its full length is uncertain. Afterward the universe went on expanding, but more slowly. The field thought to drive it is a hypothetical one called the inflaton, and the particle physics behind it is still unknown.

paragraphs.heading: From tiny patch to seeds
paragraphs.text: All the mass and energy in every galaxy now visible was packed into a sphere with a radius of about 4 × 10⁻²⁹ m, which grew to a radius of about 0.9 m by the end of inflation. The expansion supercooled the universe. It ended when the energy of the driving field turned into hot, dense particles, a step called reheating, leading to a quark-soup phase. That soup kept small differences in density, left by quantum fluctuations in the original small, smooth patch. Blown up to cosmic size, those fluctuations became the seeds from which structure in the universe grew.

paragraphs.heading: The gaps it fills
paragraphs.text: Inflation answers several problems in Big Bang cosmology that came to light in the 1970s. The Big Bang model explained the cosmic microwave background and the making of the primordial elements, but only by assuming starting conditions that were hard to justify. Stars form when gravity pulls mass into clumps, and that needs some places to be denser than others; a perfectly even spread has nothing to start the clumping. Random variations in density could do it, but the expansion pulls matter apart before it can gather into a star. Without another source of variation, Big Bang models could not make stars.

paragraphs.heading: Guth and the missing monopoles
paragraphs.text: The particle physicist Alan Guth first proposed inflation in 1979 while asking why no magnetic monopoles are seen today. Grand Unified Theories, which hold that at high temperatures the electromagnetic, strong and weak forces arise from a single theory, predict heavy, stable particles never found in nature. The most notorious is the magnetic monopole, a stable, heavy charge of magnetic field, which should have been made in such numbers that it would now be the main ingredient of the universe. Yet every search has failed. Guth found that a positive-energy false vacuum would, under general relativity, cause exponential expansion of space. Inflation below the temperature where monopoles can form would spread them apart as space grew, cutting their density by many orders of magnitude.

paragraphs.heading: The flatness problem
paragraphs.text: Inflation also solves the flatness problem and, above all, the horizon problem. The flatness problem, also called the oldness problem, is a fine-tuning puzzle in the Big Bang model. Observations of the cosmic microwave background show the universe is flat to within a few percent. In standard cosmology, the density of matter and energy shapes the curvature of space-time, and a flat universe needs one very specific critical density. The density observed today sits very close to that critical value.

paragraphs.heading: Evidence and doubts
paragraphs.text: Many physicists think inflation also explains why the universe looks the same in all directions, why the cosmic microwave background is spread evenly, why the universe is flat, and why monopoles have never turned up. Some of its predictions have been borne out: temperature differences seen by the COBE satellite in 1992 had the nearly scale-invariant pattern inflation predicts, and WMAP results also give strong evidence for it. Still, some scientists disagree. The theory took shape in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and Alexei Starobinsky, Alan Guth and Andrei Linde shared the 2014 Kavli Prize for pioneering it.
